The declaration file for the .mjs checker. Repo convention pairs every scripts/*.mjs with a .d.mts so TypeScript consumers see its API; the registry named only the runtime half.
The canonical layer sequence and edge-classification rules must[0] is about. The registry declared the scanner (a later stage) and not the contract module the scanner applies.
The scenario table the fault-matrix cases enumerate. A benchmark scenario list is neither test nor product source, and the registry file list has no benchmarks/ entry at all.
The published ./invariant companion. Package rules require the companion to live beside the manifest module it observes; the registry declared the manifest module alone.
The consumer that reads recorded provenance in production. must[2] is about verification reaching a real inventory, and the inventory is where that call site lives.

HOT ZONE. Written from `git show 05c22146ef -- packages/kernel/trust-kernel/src/index.ts` (+42/-1): `createTrustKernel` takes a new `config: TrustKernelConfig` carrying `trustAnchors`, a module-private `CONFIGURED_ANCHORS` WeakMap keyed by the handle holds them, and `configuredTrustAnchors` is a new export. That is a change to construction, not a read of it. The WeakMap keying is the load-bearing part: only a caller already holding the unforgeable handle can read the anchors, and a forged object reaches nothing because it was never a key. `createTrustKernel` still performs no I/O — the boot path reads configuration and passes the result — so the constructor stays total. An earlier version of this entry said P1-02 only READS `signatureRoots` and does not change construction, which was simply false.
Candidate-lock construction, which is half of must[0]: a lock that pins integrity has to be built somewhere, and the registry declared only the comparison side.
The atomic commit path. must[0] requires the lock to be written durably; the registry named the decision functions and not the write.
The boot-admission decision the U stage proves. The registry declared the lock package broadly and this file is where admission is decided.

The structural gate §12.1 substituted for the withdrawn fetch-spy assertion: the boot closure contains no HTTP client. It is program infrastructure the epic was told to build, not product code.
The provider whose filesystem access the trust decision gates. The clause is about what a skill may reach, and this is the reaching.
The local trust store the decision reads. The registry declared the policy and not the store it consults.

Written from `git show c3992e5124 -- apps/cli/src/profile-boot.ts` (+52/-3): profile boot imports `negotiateProfileLayerCompatibility` and `DSH_RUNTIME_API_VERSION`, runs the negotiation on the admitted layers before any patch reaches `boot()`, and the result gains a `compatBlockedLayers` field whose layers are absent from `bundlePatches` — so a blocked layer's plugin code never mounts (acceptance[1]). It is in this epic's scope because the clause is about boot ADMISSION: proving it in the solver alone would leave the refusal unreached by any launch.
The runtime guard that attributes a tool call to its owning plugin. Ownership is decided here, and the registry named only the attribution rules.
The host runner entry that installs the guard above. Its registration is what puts attribution on the live path.
The catalog surface whose entries carry owner attribution to the model.
The generator that produces the catalog the case reads. A generated artifact cannot be frozen without naming its generator.
The published ./invariant companion for the principal package, required beside the module it observes.

Written from `git show 1ac2dfe4d1 -- packages/kernel/trust-kernel/src/index.ts` (+31/-5): the module imports `generateKeyPairSync`/`sign`/`verify` from node:crypto, mints an Ed25519 keypair per kernel, and holds it in a module-private WeakMap keyed by the handle — so the PRIVATE key is never a property of `signatureRoots`, which crosses the plugin boundary. `signWithSignatureRoots`/`verifyWithSignatureRoots` are new exports, and a handle this module did not mint is refused rather than handed an empty signature. This replaced a four-byte constant that was identical in every installation, so any deployment's token verified anywhere and verification could not fail (P2-02 must[1]). Construction changed here under P2-02's acceptance lock, and the lift records the same facts.

Created by this epic under §12.11: the actor resolution and the idempotency-key derivation both execution paths need. Not a hot zone — a new file in the package that already owns the manifest — but recorded because the plan named neither. It exists rather than living in each caller for the reason BLOCKED-136 measures: two paths deriving the same key is one rule with two implementations, and the derivation IS the contract (a replayed attempt keys the same, a new one does not).

HOT ZONE. Written from `git show ed09684ecf -- packages/core/session/src/index.ts` (+24/-0): the Session log gains a private `typeCounts` Map, maintained on every append, and a public `countEventsOfType(type)` reading it. Why: must[1] needs the manifest `sequence` to be one running position across two call sites (the native tool path and the PTC code-mode sub-dispatch), and a per-append counter avoids the O(n) scan a hot path would pay per operation. The method is deliberately generic — this Session names no manifest — because the event map is merge-extended downstream and a manifest-specific counter here would invert that dependency. An earlier version of this entry said the epic "contributes an event type and does not change the log itself", which described the declaration merging in dsh-action-manifest and hid this file's actual change.

The session log as a real `ManifestAppender`. `appendManifestThenGate` is the one implementation of must[1]'s construct-append-gate order and the whole of must[2]'s no-bypass argument, and it needs a sink; the only one shipped was in-memory, so both dispatch paths wrote the order out for themselves and the shared implementation had no caller (§12.33). It lives in `dsh-tools` rather than in `dsh-action-manifest` because a capability definition reaching for a session is the edge BLOCKED-136 records, and `dsh-tools` is already the runtime side both paths import.

§12.48-B(a), §12.49(4) step 1. The three preset approval thresholds. Zero behaviour change while the dispatch gate is unwired, and landing it first keeps the gate slice from carrying a profile change too.
§12.50. The native dispatch path calls the gate before taking a ledger reservation.
§12.50. The Consumer role: the gate must sit where both dispatch paths reach it, and this module already holds the reserve/confirm pair for that reason (§12.35-2).

§12.48-B(b). The registry's U list names `core/tools/src/types.ts`, but the tool DEFINITION lives here — `types.ts` in that package holds only PTC event payloads. `riskDomainTags` is declared on `ToolDefinition`, which is what the dispatch gate will classify from.
§12.50. The code-mode dispatch path calls the SAME gate, which is what makes acceptance[0]'s cross-surface consistency hold by construction.
§12.48-B(b). `defineTool` is here, and a declared tag that the builder drops would satisfy the textual structural gate while reaching no runtime.
The dependency edge the Provider role adds: permission-presets on risk-taxonomy.

§12.47(i). The registry's P-stage list named only `risk-taxonomy/src/index.ts`, which makes the Provider stage a barrel edit and leaves the capability seam without a Provider: `classify` takes the organisation policy as a PARAMETER, so nothing classifies anything until a mount binds it. The binding belongs where the deployment's other permission knobs live — `permission-presets` already owns `approval/policy` — giving Definition (risk-taxonomy vocabulary + `classify`) / Provider (this file, holding and validating the `RiskPolicy`) / Consumer (the dispatch gate, U stage). The plan listed one file because it had not applied the capability-seam rule, not because the Provider role was meant to be absent.
§12.50. The gate's cases live with the policy package because the core reads the policy through a structural port; a test inside the core could only mount a fake.

The Provider stage's own cases. They test the BINDING — that the mounted policy is what classifies, that the threshold is the deployment's, and that a policy switching off a kernel hard-deny is refused at mount — rather than re-testing `classify`'s rules, which are the Contract stage's.
The project reference for the same edge.
Created by this epic under ruling §12.5 B: the single (id, epoch) rule both consumers now import, replacing two implementations (BLOCKED-136). The plan predates the finding.
The new package barrel, forced by the repository convention that every packages/*/* directory carries an index.ts entry (B4(f) scaffold).

P5-11 OWNS THIS FILE. Changed here so its second copy of the dedup rule becomes an import of the shared one; the mailbox keeps its own address check and its exported names, and P5-11's four live frozen cases pass unchanged in the same observation (BLOCKED-059 precedent).
The barrel that publishes `DuplicateArrivalError`, the refusal a caller must be able to catch. NOT labelled HOT ZONE: it gains two export lines and no behaviour.
The durable store must[0] names: one BEGIN IMMEDIATE over the domain event, its outbox rows and the inbox claim. Created by this epic after the clause was reworded (C13) to exclude the KV seam.
The dispatch loop that turns outbox rows into delivery attempts, which is the at-least-once half of the clause.

must[2]'s production call site: a real mailbox arrival decided against the durable consumed set. It lives in this package rather than in dsh-mailbox because the store is orchestration-runtime and the mailbox is a capability definition (ruling §12.5 B).

The in-memory bus, added when §12.40 made the bus a hard dependency of every subagent composition: requiring a SQLite file for that would have put a temporary directory into thirty-eight unit suites whose subject is not durability. The same split `dsh-lease` makes against `dsh-lease-sqlite`.

The bus as a mounted service. `openBusStore` had no production caller and no plugin, so every consumer would have decided for its callers where the bus lives — and that directory is the whole of whether a bus connects two hosts at all. The plan named the decisions and the store, not the mount.

Declares `messageBus` as an injected dependency, which is what puts the manager's drain inside the bus's lifetime and, through the service value that inject delivers, lets a settlement be committed during teardown (§12.40, §12.42).

The send side's producer. The outbox decisions ran over records nothing created — `dispatchOnce`'s only caller shipped in no bundle — while the one real handoff between agents was delivered by hand and dropped whenever the parent could not receive it. This commits the settlement before anyone tries to deliver it.

Where the authority is actually presented: the dispatcher refuses a fenced or lease-refused run before a single tool runs, and writes the model-visible result that says which. A rule with no dispatch site refuses nothing, and the plan named no dispatch site.

Declares `Agent.leaseRefused`, the marker that made a refused lease distinguishable from a composition with no Run Service. The plan named the lease store and the fencing rule; the agent field is where the refusal has to be visible, because the dispatcher reads the agent rather than calling back into the Run Service (that would be a cycle).

The Run Service is the holder (§12.19-3): it takes the lease before registering the Run, renews it, releases it, and — since §12.31-A — marks the agent when the store refuses. The plan named the lease library and not the service that holds a lease.

The engine plugin, where the lease is ACQUIRED — before the worker thread exists. Acquiring after the thread starts would leave a window in which two hosts both run the script, and no later fencing check undoes it: a refused write does not un-send what the worker already did. The heartbeat and the write guard deliberately do NOT live here; gate (u) refused an earlier version that put them in the plugin, and it was right on the design too, since the lease lifetime is the run lifetime. `leaseMs`/`heartbeatMs` are Config fields added in the same change.

Created by this epic in the U rebuild (§12.15-2): the run-side view of a lease — acquire, renew, and may-I-write. It exists rather than living inline in `host.ts` so `mayWrite` reads through the lease package’s own `checkFencing` instead of comparing epochs again; a second implementation of "is this token current" would be BLOCKED-136’s shape on the check that decides whether a stale worker may write.

Two additions to `WorkflowErrorCode`: `LEASE_STORE_UNAVAILABLE` and `RUN_HELD_BY_ANOTHER_HOST`. No existing member changed. They belong to the seam DEFINITION rather than to the worker-thread provider because the code union is the seam vocabulary — a provider inventing its own codes would make the seam callers switch on strings the definition does not know — and acceptance[2] needs a caller to tell a store outage from an ordinary refusal, which an untyped throw cannot carry. The NestedStart / NestedSettled / NestedRefused messages. A nested run has to be started by the HOST, so the worker's request and the host's single reply need wire shapes; the file's existing tags are untouched.

`ChildPort` gains `startNested` and `NestedStartRequest` is declared. The port is how a script's hook reaches the host, and the plan named the runtime and session files without naming the seam between them.

The reserve/confirm pair and the refusal text, moved out of the agent loop so BOTH dispatch paths reach one implementation. The plan named the ledger and the native loop; it named no home for a rule the code-mode path also has to obey, and writing it twice is the shape BLOCKED-136 records.

Passes the registry's own context to the code-mode transport, which is what the reservation reads the ledger from. A sub-dispatch's agent handle need not carry a context, and reading one there threw inside `commit` — surfacing as hung cases rather than an error.

The code-mode dispatch site: where a sub-call reserves before running and settles after. Without it acceptance[0]'s at-most-once held for a tool called natively and not for the same tool called from a code-mode program.

The promotion rule itself. §12.25-1 declared the table shared between the router and the inbox; §12.37 corrected what it contains, and the file is where 'only a cancel is promoted' is stated once for both consumers.

The router that applies those decisions, created by this epic as the Provider half.

The board's Cordis plugin. The durable store existed as `openTaskStore(directory)` only, so every consumer would have decided for its callers where tasks live -- and the directory IS the setting acceptance[0] turns on, since two hosts contend only when a profile pointed them at one board. The durable board's implementation. It was `src/index.ts` until §12.27-1 made that file the Cordis plugin, so the store moved down one file and the same code is now cited under the new name.

The producer the epic lacked. P5-11's plan named the primitives and the consumers but nothing that CREATES a task, which is why every clause subject had zero production callers (BLOCKED-154). Delegation is the moment the ruling names, and this plugin is the seam's Consumer role: it turns `subagent/start` and `subagent/end` into a claim and a receipt. It is a new package rather than an edit to `dsh-subagent` because the claim lease is a deployment-varying setting and `SubagentRuntime` has no Config to carry one.
